content: 1. Health systems should aim to provide equitable musculoskeletal healthcare, as highlighted in the Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy in 2023 (Volume 53, Pages 162-171). 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a framework for integrated, people-centered health services, which can be accessed through their official repository. 3. WHO has also introduced a framework for meaningful engagement of individuals living with noncommunicable diseases, mental health conditions, and neurological disorders, emphasizing the importance of patient involvement in healthcare planning and delivery. 4. An international survey conducted by Swain et al. in 2014, published in BMC Public Health, explored the prevalence and characteristics of pain in adolescents, providing valuable insights into this population's health challenges. 5. Hestbaek et al. (2006) conducted an eight-year follow-up study on 9600 twins, examining the progression of low back pain from adolescence to adulthood, as published in the journal Spine. 6. Lyng et al. (2023) systematically reviewed the evidence and identified gaps in the understanding of chronic musculoskeletal pain, as published in the journal Pain (Volume 164, Pages 1406-1415). 7. Suman et al. (2021) conducted a systematic review on the effectiveness of mass media campaigns for managing low back pain, published in Disability and Rehabilitation (Volume 43, Pages 3523-3551). 8. O’Sullivan et al. (2020) outlined ten essential facts about back pain that every individual should know, emphasizing evidence-based approaches to management, as published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine (Volume 54, Pages 698-699). 9. Hayden et al. (2021) performed a network meta-analysis to determine which types of exercise are most effective for individuals with chronic low back pain, as published in the Journal of Physiotherapy (Volume 67, Pages 252-262). 10. WHO has issued guidelines for the non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults, focusing on primary and community care settings. 11. Chou et al. (2018) conducted a systematic scoping review to understand patients' perceived needs for allied health and complementary medicine in managing low back pain, as published in Health Expectations (Volume 21, Pages 824-847). 12. Chiarotto et al. (2018) identified core outcome measurement instruments for clinical trials in nonspecific low back pain, as published in the journal Pain (Volume 159, Pages 481-495). 13. Dworkin et al. (2005) provided recommendations for core outcome measures in chronic pain clinical trials through the IMMPACT initiative, as published in the journal Pain (Volume 113, Pages 9-19). 14. Ashton-James et al. (2022) emphasized the importance of considering social outcomes in pain management research and practice, beyond just pain, distress, and disability, as published in the journal Pain (Volume 163, Pages e426-e431). 15. Hickey et al. (2023) evaluated the content validity of patient-reported outcome measures for individuals with chronic pain, emphasizing the importance of incorporating the patient’s perspective, as published in the journal Pain (Volume 164, Pages 252-257). 16. Gorrell et al. (2023) updated a systematic review on the reporting of adverse events associated with spinal manipulation in randomized clinical trials, as published in BMJ Open (Volume 13, Article e067526). 17. The GRADE evidence certainty criteria define the confidence levels in trial results, considering factors such as risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, and publication bias. High certainty indicates strong confidence in the true effect being close to the estimated effect, while very low certainty reflects significant uncertainty. 18. Trials evaluating systemic pharmacotherapy agents for chronic pain have varied in participant demographics, treatment durations, and dosages. For example, opioid agonists, partial agonists, and mixed agents have been studied with treatment durations ranging from 4 to 16 weeks. 19. Herbal medicine trials have evaluated agents such as cayenne pepper, devil's claw, and white willow bark for managing chronic pain. These trials have assessed various formulations, dosages, and application methods, with treatment durations typically lasting several weeks. 20. WHO guidelines for non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain emphasize the importance of standardized education, advice, and evidence-based interventions, considering factors such as benefits, harms, costs, equity, and feasibility.
